question: What is Hibernate and how does it relate to JPA?
title: Hibernate and JPA Relationship Explained
direct_answer: **Hibernate** is an **ORM framework** and the most popular **JPA implementation**. **JPA is the specification** (interfaces and annotations); Hibernate provides the concrete code that fulfils it. Spring Boot's `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` ships **Hibernate as the default provider**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can separate the JPA specification from the Hibernate implementation and explain why coding to the spec matters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 'JPA' and 'Hibernate' interchangeably without realising JPA is only the interface contract
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that coding against jakarta.persistence interfaces lets you swap Hibernate for EclipseLink without touching entity code

sections.title: Understanding JPA Specification vs Hibernate Implementation
sections.content:
**JPA (Java Persistence API)** is a specification — a set of interfaces and rules that define how Java objects map to database tables. It's a contract. **Hibernate** is the concrete code that fulfils that contract: it's like the difference between an architectural blueprint (JPA) and the house built from it (Hibernate).

**ORM (Object-Relational Mapping)** means automatically converting Java objects to database rows and back, removing manual JDBC code. When you use Spring Data JPA, you write against JPA interfaces like `EntityManager` and annotations like `@Entity`, but **Hibernate runs underneath** doing the real database work. Because you depend on the spec, you could swap to another provider like **EclipseLink** without changing your code. In Spring Boot, adding `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` bundles Hibernate as the default — you don't choose it explicitly.

sections.title: JPA vs Hibernate at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|JPA specification|~The contract|jakarta.persistence interfaces|@Entity, EntityManager|defines behavior, no engine
blue|Hibernate|~The implementation|generates real SQL|dirty checking, caching|default in Spring Boot
emerald|Spring Data JPA|~Repository layer|extends JpaRepository|derived queries|sits on top of both
violet|Portability|~Swap providers|code to the spec|EclipseLink, OpenJPA|entities stay unchanged

sections.title: Entity Using JPA Annotations (Hibernate Executes)
When This Distinction Matters
sections.content:
Use **JPA annotations** (`@Entity`, `@Id`, `@ManyToOne`) for all standard mapping — this keeps your code portable. Reach for **Hibernate-specific features** only when JPA lacks something: custom types with `@Type`, formula columns with `@Formula`, or specific caching strategies.

The distinction also matters when debugging: `org.hibernate` in a stack trace means you're seeing Hibernate internals, while `jakarta.persistence` is the JPA layer. JPA docs tell you what's portable across providers; Hibernate docs show extras specific to that engine.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mixing terminology** — saying 'JPA generates the query' when it's Hibernate doing the work; JPA only defines the rules.
- **Importing Hibernate classes directly** — using `org.hibernate.Session` in service code instead of `jakarta.persistence.EntityManager` ties you to Hibernate needlessly.
- **Thinking they're inseparable** — you could run EclipseLink or OpenJPA instead, because your code targets the spec.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JPA** is the specification — interfaces like `EntityManager` and annotations like `@Entity`.
- **Hibernate** is the most widely used implementation of that specification.
- **ORM** maps Java objects to database rows automatically, removing manual JDBC.
- **`spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`** brings the JPA interfaces plus Hibernate as the default provider.
- **Package tells the layer** — `jakarta.persistence` is JPA; `org.hibernate` is Hibernate-specific.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JPA is the specification and Hibernate is the implementation. Think of JPA as the blueprint — it defines the interfaces and annotations, like the Entity annotation and the EntityManager interface, that describe how persistence should work. Hibernate is the actual builder that follows that blueprint and does the work.

When you add the spring-boot-starter-data-jpa dependency to a Spring Boot project, you get both: the JPA interfaces you code against, plus Hibernate running behind the scenes. This separation is powerful because you're writing to a standard. If you ever needed to, you could swap Hibernate for another JPA provider like EclipseLink without changing your code. In practice Hibernate is so dominant that most projects just use it.

The key thing is knowing which layer you're touching. When you annotate a class with the Entity annotation, that's JPA. Hibernate reads it and generates the actual SQL. A common fresher mistake is importing org dot hibernate classes directly in service code when they should stick to the jakarta persistence imports to keep things standard. In an interview, showing you understand this specification-versus-implementation distinction proves you know the architecture, not just the syntax.

question: What is the Hibernate Session and how does it relate to JPA EntityManager?
title: Hibernate Session vs JPA EntityManager
direct_answer: **Hibernate Session** is Hibernate's native API; **JPA EntityManager** is the standardized equivalent from the spec. Hibernate implements `EntityManager` by wrapping its `Session` internally, so both drive the **same persistence context**. In Spring Boot you inject `EntityManager`; you can `unwrap(Session.class)` for Hibernate-only features.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that Session and EntityManager are two APIs over the same persistence context, and which to prefer
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realising Session and EntityManager manage the same underlying persistence context
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that EntityManager wraps Session and you can unwrap it to reach Hibernate-specific methods without abandoning the standard

sections.title: Two APIs for the Same Persistence Context
sections.content:
**Hibernate Session** is Hibernate's original API, created before JPA existed. **JPA EntityManager** is the standardized interface defined by the JPA specification. Both manage the **persistence context** — the in-memory cache of entities and their lifecycle.

Think of them as two remote controls for the same TV: Session is Hibernate's original remote with extra buttons; EntityManager is the universal remote that works with any JPA provider. When you call `entityManager.persist(customer)`, Hibernate's EntityManager delegates to its internal Session. In Spring Boot you inject EntityManager because it's portable; in legacy Hibernate apps, or when you need a stateless session, you'd use Session directly. The underlying persistence context is identical.

sections.title: Session vs EntityManager at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|EntityManager|~JPA standard|jakarta.persistence|portable across providers|inject in Spring Boot
blue|Session|~Hibernate native|org.hibernate.Session|extra Hibernate features|legacy or special cases
emerald|Persistence context|~Shared underneath|same in-memory cache|both manage it|one TV, two remotes
violet|unwrap()|~Bridge between them|entityManager.unwrap(Session.class)|reach Hibernate methods|keep the rest standard

sections.title: Using EntityManager in Spring Boot (Standard JPA)
When to Use Each API
sections.content:
Use **EntityManager** in all Spring Boot apps — it's the standard JPA interface and keeps code portable. Spring Data JPA repositories use it internally, so this covers almost everything.

Use **Session directly** only for legacy Hibernate projects, Hibernate-only features like stateless sessions for batch processing, or custom interceptors. Even then, prefer `entityManager.unwrap(Session.class)` so the rest of your code stays standard.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using Session in Spring Boot** — injecting Session directly because of an old tutorial, when EntityManager is the modern standard.
- **Not knowing they're related** — treating Session and EntityManager as unrelated systems when they share one persistence context.
- **Afraid to unwrap** — not realising `entityManager.unwrap(Session.class)` lets you reach Hibernate features without abandoning JPA.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Hibernate Session** is Hibernate's original native API, predating JPA.
- **JPA EntityManager** is the standardized interface every provider must implement.
- **Both manage the same persistence context** — different APIs over one in-memory cache.
- **Prefer `@PersistenceContext EntityManager`** in Spring for portability.
- **`entityManager.unwrap(Session.class)`** reaches Hibernate-only features when needed.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Session is Hibernate's native API and EntityManager is the JPA standard interface, but they both manage the same persistence context underneath. Hibernate created Session back in the early two-thousands, before JPA was standardized. When JPA came along, Hibernate implemented the EntityManager interface by wrapping its own Session internally. So when you call entity manager dot persist, Hibernate's implementation forwards that to its Session to do the real work.

In Spring Boot you always inject EntityManager using the PersistenceContext annotation, because that's the portable, standard way. If you were writing a plain Hibernate application, you'd get a SessionFactory and pull a Session from it.

The nice thing is you don't have to choose exclusively. If you need a Hibernate-specific feature, like a stateless session for batch processing, you can unwrap the EntityManager to get the underlying Session, and keep the rest of your code on the standard. Most freshers don't realise these are related — they think Session and EntityManager are two completely different systems, when really they're two remotes for the same TV. The mistake to avoid is reaching for Session directly in Spring Boot services, because that ties your code to Hibernate when you should be coding to the JPA standard.

question: What is Hibernate's first-level cache?
title: Hibernate First-Level Cache Explained
direct_answer: Hibernate's **first-level cache** is the **persistence context** — an in-memory cache scoped to a single `Session`/transaction. Loading the same entity by ID twice in one transaction returns the **cached instance** instead of re-querying. It's **always enabled and not configurable**, and it guarantees entity identity within the transaction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Hibernate's transaction-scoped caching and the identity guarantee it provides
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the first-level cache (always on, per-transaction) with the second-level cache (optional, cross-transaction)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the first-level cache guarantees == identity within a transaction and prevents duplicate SELECTs

sections.title: Transaction-Scoped In-Memory Entity Cache
sections.content:
**Hibernate's first-level cache** is the persistence context — an in-memory map of entities loaded during the current transaction. Every **Session**/**EntityManager** has its own. When you load an entity by ID, Hibernate stores it; load the same entity again in the same transaction and Hibernate returns the cached instance without re-querying.

Think of it as a shopping basket: within your session you see the same items you added; once you check out (commit), the basket is cleared. The cache gives you **performance** (no redundant SELECTs) and **consistency** (multiple references to one entity are the same Java object). It's always enabled, mandatory, and lives and dies with the transaction.

sections.title: First-Level Cache at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Scope|~Per transaction|tied to one Session|cleared on commit|new request = new cache
blue|Always on|~Not configurable|can't disable it|mandatory in Hibernate|free performance
emerald|Identity guarantee|~Same Java object|two finds, one instance|== returns true|changes seen everywhere
rose|Batch risk|~Memory bloat|thousands of entities|flush() and clear()|avoid OutOfMemoryError

sections.title: First-Level Cache in Action
When First-Level Cache Matters
sections.content: You never 'turn on' the first-level cache — it's always working. But it matters in several places: loading the same entity twice in a method means only the first call hits the database; modifying one reference updates the other because they're the same instance; calling `entityManager.refresh(entity)` forces a reload from the database. In batch jobs loading thousands of entities in one transaction, the cache grows large, so you flush and clear periodically. Because the cache is per-transaction, data isn't shared across web requests.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing it with the second-level cache** — first-level is per-transaction and always on; second-level is cross-transaction, optional, and configured separately.
- **Expecting cross-request caching** — loading a customer in one request won't be cached in another; the cache clears at commit.
- **Not clearing in batch jobs** — processing 10,000 rows in one transaction without `flush()` and `clear()` bloats the cache into an OutOfMemoryError.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **First-level cache** is the persistence context, scoped to one Session/transaction.
- It's **always enabled** and cannot be turned off or configured.
- **Identity guarantee** — repeated loads of one ID return the same Java object (`==` is true).
- It's **cleared on commit/rollback**, so entities become detached afterward.
- In **batch jobs**, call `flush()` and `clear()` to avoid memory bloat.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The first-level cache is Hibernate's transaction-scoped in-memory cache. Every EntityManager or Session has one, and it's always on. When you load an entity by ID, Hibernate stores it in this cache. If you load that same entity again in the same transaction, Hibernate just returns the cached instance — no second database query.

This does two things. First, it's faster, because you avoid redundant queries. Second, it guarantees that within a transaction, all references to the same entity point to the exact same Java object. So if you change one reference, every other reference sees that change immediately, because they're literally the same object in memory.

The cache is cleared when the transaction ends. So if you load a customer in one request, then load it again in a different request, that's a brand new transaction with a fresh cache, and you'll hit the database both times.

The thing freshers confuse is first-level versus second-level cache. First-level is per-transaction and always on. Second-level is optional, shared across transactions, and needs explicit configuration. And in batch jobs, if you load thousands of entities in one transaction, the first-level cache can grow huge and cause memory problems, so you call flush and then clear periodically to empty it.

question: What is the N+1 query problem in Hibernate?
title: Hibernate N+1 Query Problem
direct_answer: The **N+1 problem** is when loading N parent entities triggers **1 query for the parents plus N queries for their lazy children** — e.g. 10 orders cause 11 queries instead of 1. The root cause is **lazy loading** firing one query per access. Fix it with **JOIN FETCH** or **@EntityGraph**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognise the most common JPA performance bug and can both detect and fix it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not noticing N+1 because tests run on tiny datasets, or 'fixing' it by switching everything to EAGER
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show you detect N+1 with show-sql and fix it selectively with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or @BatchSize

sections.title: The Most Common JPA Performance Problem
sections.content:
The **N+1 query problem** is when loading a parent entity with a lazy collection makes Hibernate run 1 query for the parents plus N more — one per child — instead of a single JOIN. Load 10 orders with `SELECT * FROM orders` (1 query), then iterate and access `order.getItems()`, and Hibernate fires a separate query for each order's items (10 queries). Total: 11 instead of 1.

It's called N+1 because it's N (parents) + 1 (the initial query). It's insidious because tests with 3 orders only make 4 queries — barely noticeable. In production with 1,000 orders you run 1,001 queries and the app crawls. **Lazy loading** is the root cause: Hibernate doesn't load children until you touch them.

sections.title: N+1 vs JOIN FETCH
sections.content:
| Aspect | Lazy access (N+1) | JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph |
|---|---|---|
| Queries for 10 parents | 11 (1 + 10) | 1 |
| Trigger | Accessing each lazy collection | Single query up front |
| Scales to 1,000 parents | 1,001 queries | 1 query |
| Risk | Silent in tests, slow in prod | Loads only what you ask for |
| How to detect | `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` | n/a — already fixed |

sections.title: N+1 at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Root cause|~Lazy loading|children loaded on access|one query each|default for collections
blue|Symptom|~Query flood|1 + N queries|grows with data|invisible on tiny tests
emerald|JOIN FETCH|~JPQL fix|single JOIN query|loads parent + children|use when you need them
violet|Detect it|~show-sql|see every query|spot repeated SELECTs|profile before prod

sections.title: Without — Lazy Access Fires N+1 Queries
With — JOIN FETCH Loads Everything in One Query
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not detecting it** — testing with 2-3 rows and never enabling SQL logging, so the query flood goes unnoticed. Always turn on `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` in development.
- **Going EAGER globally** — switching `@OneToMany(fetch = EAGER)` to dodge N+1 means you always load children even when unneeded. Use JOIN FETCH selectively per query instead.
- **Lazy access outside the transaction** — touching a lazy collection after the transaction closes throws `LazyInitializationException`; the fix is fetching it in the query, not making everything EAGER.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **N+1** = 1 query for N parents plus N queries for children, instead of a single JOIN.
- **Root cause** is lazy loading firing one query per collection access.
- **Detect it** with `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` — a flood of similar SELECTs is the signal.
- **JOIN FETCH** (JPQL) or **@EntityGraph** loads parents and children in one query.
- **Don't go EAGER globally** — fetch selectively only where you need the children.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The N plus one problem is when you load a parent entity and Hibernate fires a separate query for each child collection, instead of loading everything in one go. Here's a concrete example. Say you load ten orders from the database — that's one query. Each order has a list of items that's loaded lazily. When you loop through the orders and call get items, Hibernate runs a separate query for each order's items. That's ten more queries. So you end up with eleven queries total, when you could have done it all in one with a JOIN.

This is brutal in production. With a thousand orders you're running a thousand and one queries, and the app slows to a crawl.

The fix is to use JOIN FETCH in your JPQL query. You write SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o dot items, and now Hibernate generates a single SQL query with a join and loads everything at once. Another option is the EntityGraph annotation on your repository method, where you declare which associations to load eagerly.

The key mistake freshers make is not detecting this. They test with three orders, see four queries, and think it's fine. Turn on show sql in your application properties — if you see a flood of similar queries, that's N plus one. And don't fix it by making everything eager fetch, because that loads children even when you don't need them. Fetch selectively with JOIN FETCH or EntityGraph only where you know you'll use the data.

question: How does Hibernate generate SQL from entity classes?
title: How Hibernate Generates SQL
direct_answer: At **startup**, Hibernate scans `@Entity` classes and reads annotations like `@Table`, `@Column`, and `@Id` to build an **internal metadata model** (the SessionFactory). From that metadata it generates **dialect-specific SQL** for CRUD (and DDL if `ddl-auto` is set). The configured **Hibernate Dialect** adapts the syntax per database.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that Hibernate builds a metadata model at startup and emits dialect-specific SQL, not runtime code parsing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Hibernate parses Java code at runtime instead of reading annotations once at startup
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Hibernate dialects and how they give database portability without changing entity code

sections.title: How Hibernate Translates Java Objects to SQL
sections.content:
Hibernate is an **ORM** framework that removes manual JDBC by generating SQL from your entity classes. At application startup, it scans classes annotated with **@Entity** and reads metadata from **@Table**, **@Column**, **@Id**, **@OneToMany**, **@ManyToOne**, and so on.

This metadata builds an internal **SessionFactory** holding the object-to-table mappings. When you call `entityManager.persist(user)` or `userRepository.save(user)`, Hibernate consults the mapping and generates the right INSERT, UPDATE, SELECT, or DELETE. The SQL is **dialect-specific** — a configured **Hibernate Dialect** adapts syntax for PostgreSQL, MySQL, or Oracle. Hibernate is a translator: you write object-oriented code, and it emits the SQL your database understands, handling vendor quirks for you.

sections.title: SQL Generation Pipeline at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Startup scan|~Reads annotations once|@Entity, @Table, @Column|builds the metadata model|restart to pick up changes
blue|SessionFactory|~Holds the mappings|object-to-table model|consulted per operation|generates the SQL
emerald|Dialect|~Database flavour|PostgreSQLDialect, MySQLDialect|adapts types and syntax|portability for free
violet|ddl-auto|~Schema control|validate / update / none|create drops + rebuilds|never create/update in prod

sections.title: Entity Annotations to Generated SQL
When Hibernate SQL Generation Matters
sections.content: Lean on automatic SQL generation for **CRUD-heavy apps** and **REST APIs** where Spring Data JPA derives queries from method names like `findByEmailAndActiveTrue()`. It's also key for **multi-database support**: change the dialect in `application.properties` and your app targets a different database without code changes. For **complex analytical queries** across many tables or bulk operations, write native SQL or JPQL instead of relying on generated SQL.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming runtime parsing** — Hibernate reads annotations once at startup into a static model; change an annotation and you must restart.
- **Ignoring the dialect** — without the right dialect, Hibernate may emit incompatible SQL (e.g. `LONGTEXT` on PostgreSQL, which expects `TEXT`).
- **Using `ddl-auto=update` in production** — it can cause data loss or locking; use migration tools like Flyway instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@Entity** marks a class for table mapping; Hibernate scans these at startup.
- The **Hibernate Dialect** generates database-specific SQL for types and functions.
- The **SessionFactory** holds all mappings and drives SQL generation from metadata.
- **ddl-auto** modes: create, update, validate, none — never create/update in production.
- Hibernate maps **camelCase to snake_case** by default unless `@Column(name=...)` overrides it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Hibernate generates SQL by reading entity class annotations at application startup. When you annotate a class with the Entity and Table annotations, Hibernate scans them and builds an internal metadata model that maps your Java fields to database columns. For example, if you have a Customer class with an Id field and a Column annotation on the email field, Hibernate knows it maps to a customers table with an id primary key and an email column.

When you call something like entity manager dot persist on a customer object, Hibernate looks up the mapping for that entity and generates the matching INSERT statement. The clever part is that it's dialect-specific. Hibernate uses a configured dialect class, like PostgreSQL dialect or MySQL dialect, to adapt the SQL for your database. So the same Java code produces a BIGSERIAL on PostgreSQL but an auto-increment on MySQL.

A common fresher mistake is thinking Hibernate reads your Java code at runtime to make SQL. It actually happens once at startup, when the SessionFactory is built. If you change an annotation, you have to restart the app for Hibernate to pick up the new mapping.

In a Spring Data JPA project you'd configure the dialect in application properties, with the database-platform property pointing at the dialect class. That tells Hibernate exactly which SQL flavour to generate, so it stays compatible with your database.

question: What is the difference between Hibernate's update, save, saveOrUpdate, and persist?
title: Hibernate save vs persist vs saveOrUpdate
direct_answer: **persist()** is the JPA-standard method that inserts a transient entity and returns void. **save()** is Hibernate-specific — it inserts and returns the generated ID immediately. **saveOrUpdate()** is Hibernate-specific and picks INSERT or UPDATE from entity state. In Spring Data JPA you just call **repository.save()**, which uses `persist()` or `merge()` underneath.

sections.title: Understanding Hibernate's Persistence Methods
sections.content:
Hibernate offers several ways to save entities. **`persist()`** is the JPA-standard method (EntityManager API): it inserts a **transient** entity (no ID yet) and throws if you pass a detached one. **`save()`** is Hibernate-specific (Session API): it also inserts but **returns the generated ID** immediately, handy when you need the ID right away. **`saveOrUpdate()`** is Hibernate-specific and smarter — it checks whether the entity is transient or detached and runs INSERT or UPDATE accordingly.

In modern **Spring Data JPA** you rarely call these directly. You call **`repository.save()`**, which uses `EntityManager.persist()` for new entities and `EntityManager.merge()` for existing ones — handling both insert and update without you tracking entity state.

sections.title: Persistence Method Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | persist() | save() | saveOrUpdate() |
|---|---|---|---|
| API standard | JPA (EntityManager) | Hibernate (Session) | Hibernate (Session) |
| Entity state | Must be transient | Transient or with ID | Transient or detached |
| Return value | void | the generated ID | void |
| Behavior | INSERT only | INSERT and return ID | INSERT or UPDATE |
| Spring Data JPA | Used internally for new entities | Not used directly | Not used directly |

sections.title: Entity States and Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|persist()|~JPA standard|transient only|returns void|throws on detached
blue|save()|~Hibernate native|returns the ID now|insert focused|Session API
emerald|saveOrUpdate()|~Hibernate native|state-aware|insert or update|legacy choice
violet|repository.save()|~Spring Data JPA|persist or merge|use for 99% of cases|the modern default

sections.title: Method Behaviour and the Spring Data Way
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using Hibernate Session instead of EntityManager** — calling `session.save()` in Spring services ties code to Hibernate; prefer repositories or EntityManager.
- **Calling persist() on a detached entity** — `persist()` only works on transient entities and throws otherwise; use `merge()` or `repository.save()`.
- **Assuming save() always INSERTs** — with a non-null ID, Spring Data calls `merge()`, which does a SELECT first; if it's truly new, keep the ID null to avoid the extra query.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **persist()** is JPA standard, inserts a transient entity, returns void.
- **save()** is Hibernate-specific and returns the generated ID immediately.
- **saveOrUpdate()** is Hibernate-specific and picks INSERT or UPDATE from state — rarely needed today.
- **repository.save()** uses `persist()` for new and `merge()` for existing entities based on the ID.
- Entity **states matter**: transient, persistent, detached, removed — `persist()` needs transient, `merge()` handles detached.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The main difference is between the JPA standard methods and Hibernate's own methods. The persist method is part of the JPA EntityManager API. It inserts a new entity into the database. The entity has to be transient, meaning it doesn't have an ID yet, and persist throws an exception if you pass it a detached entity. It returns nothing — it just adds the entity to the persistence context.

The save method is Hibernate-specific, from the Session API. It also inserts a new entity, but it immediately returns the generated ID. That's useful when you need the ID right away to create related entities in the same transaction.

Then there's saveOrUpdate, also Hibernate-specific, which is smarter — it checks whether the entity is new or already exists and runs an INSERT or an UPDATE accordingly.

In modern Spring Data JPA you don't use any of these directly. You just call repository dot save. Under the hood, the SimpleJpaRepository checks whether the entity has an ID and is known to the persistence context. If not, it calls persist. Otherwise it calls merge. So it handles both insert and update automatically.

The mistake freshers make is injecting a Hibernate Session directly and calling session dot save when they should use the EntityManager or, better still, just stick with Spring Data JPA repositories. That keeps the code portable and follows modern Spring Boot conventions.
